blurb: A morning glory that forms a bush instead of a vine: arching stems of narrow leaves making a broad mound, hung with 3-inch funnel flowers in pinkish-lavender with darker throats. Under it sits an enormous tuber — which is why it is drought-proof and very long-lived.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
spread: Bushy arching clump from a massive tuber; does not climb, does not spread
seasons: Lavender-purple funnel flowers June–August; arching bushy habit; dies back to the tuber in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 7,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Sandy or sandy-loam soil, per CSU; the Wildflower Center adds sandy or gravelly ground. It needs depth and drainage for the tuber more than it needs fertility.[1][3]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 3–4 ft wide. A spreading mounded plant with linear leaves and morning-glory flowers over a huge tap root — CSU notes it is long lived and wants sandy or sandy loam soils.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from midsummer through to frost; CSU records the colour as purple, pink and the height as 24–36 in tall.[1][3]
care.maintenance: The tuber is the whole story: it makes the plant drought-tolerant and long-lived, and it makes transplanting an established plant essentially impossible. Set out young stock and choose the spot once. Unlike the garden annual morning glories it is a bush, not a climber, so it needs no support.[1][3]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: Not a food in this guide. The huge root has a documented historical use on the Plains, but morning-glory-family seeds carry psychoactive alkaloids.[1][3]
edible.caution: This guide does not treat bush morning glory as food. The enormous root was known and used by Plains peoples, but that historical record is not a modern preparation guide and this entry does not present it as one. The relevant chemical caution is the family: Convolvulaceae seeds characteristically contain ergoline (lysergic-acid-amide) alkaloids, which are genuinely psychoactive and toxic in quantity — so the seeds in particular are not to be eaten, by people or pets. Grow it for the flowers and the astonishing root.[1][3]
